title: What We Still Have to Solve

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: What We Still Have to Solve asks why technological progress leaves important problems unresolved.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Its opening hospital depends on electricity, water, deliveries, trained staff, and public trust.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: A heatwave can strain several of those systems at once.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The book follows these connections instead of treating each crisis as an isolated subject.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Its distinctive question is what becomes the next constraint when an intervention succeeds.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Consider the book's example of electricity generation becoming dramatically cheaper.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: That improvement still needs grid connections, transformers, skilled crews, and workable permits.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Otherwise, falling production costs can coexist with slow connections and high household prices.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The bottleneck has moved, so buying more generation no longer addresses the whole problem.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Readers learn to distinguish missing technology from infrastructure, incentives, and authority that cannot coordinate.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The chapters follow these changing constraints through climate, health, poverty, security, and AI.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Cheap power also changes which water supplies become practical.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Desalination can expand supply, but electricity is only one requirement.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Membranes, pipelines, brine disposal, and access rules still shape the outcome.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Producing fresh water does not decide which households can receive it.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The book's method keeps those consequences inside the original promise of a solution.
